records.title: Cosmic Records — Catalogue History
records.format: Cosmic catalogue · duo mix CDs · third-party releases and remixes
records.summary: Cosmic was our label. Jeff Alderson as DJ Spice, me as DJ Friction and Voyager. COSMIC 001–018 collects that work. Transformed follows Explorations, then the duo’s releases, remixes and appearances on other labels.

items.title: October 1995
items.detail: Merritt Island, October 1995. New equipment arriving, testing it out. Groove Me came together in that first studio.

items.title: A hardware ensemble
items.detail: Bass Station Rack on the lead. Cakewalk sequencing external instruments through the Mackie 1604.

items.title: Firestone
items.detail: The promo pressing at Firestone. Hearing it in the club gave me confidence in the mix—and more freedom to write.

items.title: COSMIC 009
items.detail: You Make Me Feel So Good. A turning point in sound design and composition for me.

items.title: COSMIC 012
items.detail: The extended Ah Yeah remix. A larger console, room to see the arrangement and organize its emotional shape.

items.title: COSMIC 017
items.detail: Time Travel, my first release sequenced entirely in Logic. Alongside it, the move into digital mixing.

items.title: Release chronology
items.detail: January 1996 begins the artist-confirmed vinyl chronology. Copyright dates and provisional catalog years are not exact release dates.

sections.title: Authorized later editions and edits
sections.intro: Justin Scott Dixon confirmed authorization of these four later editions and edits on 14 October 2026. Dates and version names below follow the linked publisher or release listing.

items.title: Totemtanz — Groove Me
items.detail: TT015 / TT015X: yellow vinyl with the Original 1994 Mix, Ufo Project Remix and Bonus Beats. The printed mix name is retained; it does not replace the artist-confirmed 1996 Cosmic release chronology.

items.title: Dubvinyls — Groove Me
items.detail: Dub007 / Special Red is separate from the Voyager Recordings anniversary edition. The database classifies this pressing as unofficial; Dixon has confirmed authorization, so the two accounts are retained explicitly.

items.title: Avalon Emerson — Cybernetic Edits
items.detail: Includes Groove Me (Avalon Emerson’s Truth Of Omission Mix), a third-party edit.

items.title: Bazco & Alex Clubbers remix

sections.title: Press: contemporary review and retrospective feature

items.title: The Courier — The Rhythm
items.detail: The Courier’s dance column highlighted The Rhythm’s breakbeat sound and its progressive reverse-side mix. Published on page 6; the column’s introduction names Chris and Nik.

items.title: Forte Magazine — Millú selects Groove Me (Dub)
items.detail: Millú picked Groove Me (Dub) among five favorite 1990s rave tracks, singling out its piano break. This is a retrospective track selection, rather than a review of the anniversary edition.

items.title: The FADER — FADER Mix: Ciel
items.detail: Ciel’s published mix and interview include Future Funk and Rhythm Rockin’ in the accompanying track list.

items.title: Resident Advisor — RA.702 Or:la
items.detail: Or:la included Dark Knight in her Resident Advisor podcast. The feature documents the selection within her mix.

items.title: Resident Advisor — RA.832 Ciel
items.detail: Ciel selected You Make Me Feel So Good (Spice’s Progressive Mix) for her Resident Advisor podcast.

items.title: NTS — Kasra V with Moody Mehran
items.detail: Groove Me (1997 Remix) appears in the published episode track list.

items.title: Orlando Weekly — Fall Guide 2008: Music
items.detail: The calendar listed Friction & Spice at Club Firestone for 11 October. This is a published event announcement.

items.title: Orlando Culture Shock — Aquatic Bass 3
items.detail: A firsthand event report discusses Spice performing with Jason Brown and recalls the writer’s affection for the duo’s Step Into My Dream. The reported performance is Spice’s appearance with Jason Brown.

sections.title: Compilation reviews
sections.intro: These reviews discuss complete compilations that include the duo’s music; their praise is not attributed to an individual Friction & Spice track.

items.title: AllMusic — Funk-Da-Fried
items.detail: John Bush reviews Simply Jeff’s mix album. Its track list includes Friction & Spice’s Groove Me.

items.title: AllMusic — Electro Dance Mix
items.detail: Jason Ankeny provides an editorial overview of the compilation, whose track list includes Get Down to the Funky Beat.

sections.title: Before Cosmic: listening, performance and editing
sections.intro: Early experiences I describe in the Super Progressive interview.

items.title: Learning to listen
items.detail: Stereo was the sound stage, carefully extracted, as the fascination of how sound systems work together thru the transfer of devotion to be in control of something incredible hard to comprehend. efforts before Cosmic, became the guide book, only i knew existed.

items.title: Programming a night
items.detail: Music made for night clubs, educated the continuity with the pace of music, and how its showcased. Radio broadcast audio engineering was how marketing agents competed for more listeners , how to make music sound like it did on the radio had me hooked.

items.title: From systems to songs
items.detail: Turntables became instruments, speakers provided the bass, lighting completed the loop of futurism, manifested in the studio, destiny founded connections, partnerships of authenticity, preceded the un-needed.

items.title: Merritt Island
items.detail:
the oasis, intelligent samplers, refined synthesizers, DOS sequencers, compact consoles, cleanest signal path
Cosmic Studios became legendary, Dj's Friction and Spice, no longer secondary.

items.title: Effects as arrangement
items.detail: Delay the echo, echo the reverb, compress the ratio, attack the release. carefully Reverberation became the space, dynamic range placed it.  the arrangement was the sound, as everyone gathered around.

items.title: Larger consoles
items.detail: Cosmic 009 was the last record on the Mackie 1604. Retiring it was harder than expected, so much learning had happened across that little desk. The 24-8 brought more room, faders, routing, a meter bridge, the composition becoming something I could see across the console. The computer stayed, sixteen MIDI channels became sixty-four, the sound modules had more room to participate. Working on Aria with Rich Rosario in another studio brought ideas back to Cosmic. Ah Yeah grew through that exchange, the arrangement finding space as I learned to see its parts together.

items.title: Time Travel
items.detail: Automation and recall drew me toward the Yamaha 03D, understanding digital audio became the longer journey. Time Travel was my first release sequenced entirely in Logic, still playing the external sound modules, familiar instruments entering unfamiliar territory. Sounds were shaped at the source, but levels inside the desk needed another kind of attention. Digital overload made itself known. The Finalizer brought loudness and CD playback into the learning, clocking and synchronization took years to fully understand. I was making the equipment work before I could explain everything it was doing. The title belonged to that period, music moving alongside the technology I was trying to understand.

items.title: Aria — One
items.detail: Cass Cutbush believed in the Voyager sound. Through Fire, the opportunity came to put the original One alongside a new remix, bringing what I was learning back to a piece already familiar. Rhythm became more dependable, drums could gather in layers, longer film samples brought a cinematic space into the arrangement. Pumping effects could be shaped inside Logic, without building the process around external equipment. The studio was still part hardware, part computer, but more of the idea could develop within the session. One became a meeting point, an earlier composition heard through an expanding set of possibilities.

items.title: Software instruments
items.detail: EXS24, Absynth, ES2, EVOC. More cinematic possibilities, easier session recall.

sections.intro: My recollection of the sessions. Specific album editions and dates remain to be verified.

items.title: The phone would ring
items.detail: Usually a day or two before deadline, the phone would ring. AK1200 needed to record a set for his latest release. A vinyl acetate showcase, captured quickly in Pro Tools, working forward along the timeline.

items.title: Keep moving
items.detail: If the mix fell off, we did it again. Stitch just before the bad mix into the newly recorded attempt. Keep moving.

items.title: Listen to the end result
items.detail: Direct speaker monitoring via the TC Electronic Finalizer Plus, allowing us to simulate downstream limiting and EQ. That processing was for monitoring; not delivery...

items.title: Be his wingman
items.detail: Be Dave’s wingman, without him having to explain what was needed. That was the relationship we developed over the years. He performed; I handled the recording and edit.

items.title: It happens in the moment
items.detail: Dave needed to just do what he does. It happens in the moment—that’s his brand. Once it feels contrived, he disowns it and never looks back.

items.title: That was the world of DnB
items.detail: For me, DnB is the most cut-the-BS genre of electronic music. Always will be. Unforgiving of posers.

items.title: Mastering? Almost taboo
items.detail: Mastering? Almost taboo. Dave played acetates. As I understood it, mastering was already done at the lathe. DnB artists were fanatical about preserving it.

items.title: The edited set, without another layer
items.detail: Long-form stereo left-and-right master bounce, straight from the edit session. Bit for bit on a data disc, burned using Toast. No mastering plug-ins. No EQ. No limiters.

items.title: From us to the label
items.detail: CD mastering in-house at the label. Indexing at the duplication plant, using the text file we sent.

items.title: Almost Flew
items.detail: Almost Flew changed how I used scales. Where the vocal sat, and how new melodies could work around it.

items.title: Pulse
items.detail: A cinematic opening, then a heavier dance-floor section. Pulse let me express the compositional control I had been working toward.

items.title: Preservation
items.detail: Returning to archived hardware patches was rewarding. It also reminded me why recall mattered. Getting back into the work, practically.

historySections.title: The club, remembered in the studio
historySections.intro: Justin Scott Dixon’s recollection of working with Sandra Collins, edited for this archive.

items.title: Bringing the live experience into the room
items.detail: In the studio, there were just the two of us, drawing on the energy we remembered from the club. We had to bring that experience into a controlled room while we shaped the programme, so the mix could retain the feeling of hearing Sandra live.

items.title: An invisible language
items.detail: At times, we knew what needed to happen without putting it into words. That shared understanding was part of our collaboration, alongside the close review and editing we did together.

items.title: Listening from another room
items.detail: Sometimes one of us would step into another room, away from the main listening position. Hearing the balance of two songs from somewhere else, and briefly on our own, could reveal details we missed while immersed in the mix. Even within a close collaboration, that individual perspective mattered.
